results.title: WATCH: Adaptive Monitoring for AI Deployments via Weighted-Conformal Martingales
results.content: However, existing CTM monitoring methods (e.g., Vovk et al., (2021)) all rely on some form of exchangeability (e.g., IID) assumption in their null hypotheses—informally, meaning that the data distribution is the same across time or data batches—and as a result, standard CTMs can raise unnecessary alarms even when a shift is mild or benign (e.g., Figure 1a). For practical applications, we propose WATCH: Weighted Adaptive Testing for Changepoint Hypotheses, a framework for AI monitoring using WCTMs. WATCH continuously adapts to mild or benign distribution shifts (e.g., Figure 1a) to maintain end-user safety and utility (and avoid unnecessary alarms), while quickly detecting harmful shifts (e.g., Figure 1b & c) and enabling root-cause analysis. We now provide a worked example for how weighted-conformal -values can be used to test a common assumption in the robust ML literature: namely, the covariate shift (Shimodaira,, 2000; Sugiyama et al.,, 2007) assumption, where the marginal input distribution may shift to some other distribution at test time, but the conditional label distribution is assumed to remain invariant. Our empirical results show that WATCH’s adaptation reduces unnecessary alarms relative to standard CTMs (Vovk et al.,, 2021) while still detecting harmful shifts faster than comparable betting-based -processes that directly track the risk (i.e., from Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2021b ). In particular, Volkhonskiy et al., (2017) developed inductive CTMs (i.e., CTMs based on inductive or split conformal (Papadopoulos et al.,, 2002; Papadopoulos,, 2008)) with score and betting functions specifically taylored to fast changepoint detection; Vovk et al., (2021) proposed an approach to using standard CTMs to monitor for when a deployed AI/ML system should be retrained; and Vovk, (2021) provided a comprehensive and detailed review of CTMs as methods for testing the IID or exchangeability assumptions. As we note in the main paper, for monitoring the risk of a set-valued (e.g., conformalized) AI/ML predictor, our WCTM methods are generally more data-efficient (not requiring separate datasets for conformalization and testing, as Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2021b does); our WCTM-based Shiryaev-Roberts procedure is more computationally efficient than the compareable changepoint detection method in Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2021b (i.e., versus ); and, empirically we found that our methods often detect harmful concept shifts faster than comparable methods in Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2021b .

results.title: How do you detect label leakage in training data? | by NS Academy | Medium
results.content: # **How do you detect *label leakage* in training data?**. **Label leakage** (also called **data leakage**) happens when information from the target variable (label) is accidentally included in the input features during model training — giving the model an unfair advantage and leading to **overfitting** and **unrealistically high performance**. Here’s how to detect label leakage in training data:. Ask: *How is the data collected?* and *When are the features generated relative to the label?*. If a feature is created **after** the event you’re trying to predict, it can leak future information. For example, predicting loan default using a feature like “number of late payments in the next 3 months” is clearly leaking information from the future. * Train your model, then check **feature importances**. * If a feature has unusually high importance and it’s suspiciously correlated with the target, inspect it closely — it may be leaking label information. Check Feature Correlation with the Target. * For numeric features, calculate **Pearson/Spearman correlation** with the target. * For categorical features, use **mutual information** or **Chi-square test**. Leakage often arises from **random train-test splits** in temporal data. If features use future information not available at prediction time, splitting randomly exposes leakage. Always simulate production by splitting data **chronologically** — training on past data, testing on future data. Check if any features are just a transformed version of the label:. Look for perfect or near-perfect alignment between any feature and the label. Train a Simple Model on Just One Feature. To test individual features for leakage:. * Train a basic model (e.g., decision tree or logistic regression) using one feature at a time. * If a single feature gives unusually high predictive power, it may be leaking. Leakage-affected models perform very well in offline tests but fail in real-time scenarios. If your deployed model shows a **sharp performance drop**, you likely trained with leaked data. Data Audits and Feature Reviews. * **ETL pipelines**: Check for features that include or depend on the label. ## More from NS Academy. ## How would you perform anomaly detection on streaming data in near real-time? results.title: Covariate Shift
results.content: This shift occurs when the input variables change between training and deployment, but the relationship between input and output stays the same. Covariate shift means the input data your model sees in production does not match the input data it was trained on. This becomes a problem because machine learning models expect future data to look like past training data. With concept shift, the relationship between inputs and outputs changes. Covariate shift happens when the training data does not match the data seen during deployment. * **Sampling bias**: If your training data favors one group or behavior, your model will not perform well on others. Small changes in input can break models that rely heavily on those features. ## **How Covariate Shift Impacts Model Performance**. This can happen if the new inputs match a part of the data the model learned well. * **Use dimensionality reduction**: Tools like PCA or t-SNE can reduce your input space and reveal differences between training and live data. If the inputs have shifted, the model may no longer be solving the right problem. * **Reweight old data**: If new labels are hard to get, you can reweight your existing training data to match the new input distribution. * **Use robust models**: Tree-based models like XGBoost or Random Forests handle mild input shift better than deep networks. Covariate shift happens when the input distribution changes, but the output relationship stays the same. **Example**: A fraud model trained on weekday shopping patterns is used on holiday data. Concept shift happens when the relationship between inputs and outputs changes. * Covariate shift can be fixed by retraining or reweighting data. * Concept shift usually needs new labels or changes to how the model learns. If you fix concept shift using tools for covariate shift, you will not solve the problem. Concept shift breaks the model. It is when the inputs your model sees in production are different from what it saw during training. Covariate shift changes the inputs. Concept shift changes the meaning behind those inputs. It happens when your model sees different inputs in the real world than it saw during training. Covariate shift does not mean your model is wrong.

results.title: Covariate Shift: What it is and How to Detect it
results.content: > Covariate shift is a change in the distribution of the model’s inputs between training and production data. We are clearly experiencing a strong covariate shift; any machine learning models trained on the data from week 10 would perform very poorly on the data from week 16. In order to reliably detect covariate shift in any situation, we need (on top of the univariate methods) another method that can capture the changes in the joint distribution of all the features. > We can detect covariate shift by comparing the PCA reconstruction error from production data to its expected level. One way to estimate the expected reconstruction error is to take a portion of the training data that we know not to exhibit covariate shift (let’s call it a reference data set), split it into chunks, and compute the reconstruction error on each chunk. Then, a simple rule of thumb for declaring covariate shift is to check whether the reconstruction error from the data in production is outside of the ranges obtained from the reference set. Data drift detection based on the change in the PCA reconstruction error is no different. Then, we have said that we can use this mapping to compress and decompress data from subsequent Weeks 10 and 11 (both with no drift) and the obtained reconstruction error will be low and similar in both cases. > Our drift detector assumes that in the absence of covariate shift, reconstruction errors will be stable over time (except for the period used for learning the PCA mapping). Namely, covariate shift detection as we have done it will not capture drift when there is a non-linear transformation that preserves the correlation between features while also preserving the mean and standard deviation of each feature. Drift detection for a dataset with non-linear covariate shift that cannot be captured by PCA. Drift detection for a dataset with non-linear covariate shift that cannot be captured by PCA. While covariate shift detection through data reconstruction with PCA cannot detect some cases of shift that we have just discussed, we can detect them with univariate drift detection methods.
